# Deuteronomy 13 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Structure Overview

The chapter presents three escalating cases of enticement to idolatry, each with the same penalty (death without mercy): (1) the false prophet (vv. 1–5), (2) a close relative or friend (vv. 6–11), and (3) an entire apostate city (vv. 12–18).

**Source:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-13.html (Ellicott); https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-13-commentary (Precept Austin, citing Deere, *The Bible Knowledge Commentary*)

---

## Verses 1–5: The False Prophet

### v. 1 — *"If a prophet or dreamer of dreams arises among you and proclaims a sign or wonder…"*

- **"Prophet" (נָבִיא, nabi)** means one who speaks from God, a mouthpiece. The case here is someone *pretending* to have received divine revelation. **"Dreamer of dreams"** refers to one claiming revelation through dreams, which was a legitimate means God used (Num. 12:6) but could also be counterfeited. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/13.htm — Pulpit; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/13.htm — Gill)

- Gill adds that this is clearly a *false* prophet, a "lying prophet" as the Targum of Jonathan calls him, who pretends to be sent from God with new revelation or predictions. Dreams are also used figuratively for "false doctrines, vain, deceitful, and illusory." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/13.htm)

- David Guzik notes that dreams *can* come from God (Gen. 37:5-11; Num. 12:6) but can also be false (Jer. 23:25-26). In the Bible, God spoke to pagans/unbelievers through dreams almost twice as often as to His own people. Believers must test any dream-claim and not put too much confidence in them. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-13/)

- The NET Bible note (cited by Precept Austin) explains that the difference between a "prophet" and a "dreamer of dreams" was one of function: the prophet was more a proclaimer/interpreter, while the dreamer was a receiver of revelation. In later times, the dreamer's role was denigrated (cf. Jer. 23:28). The expression "sign or wonder" (אוֹת אוֹ מוֹפֵת) became a formulaic way of authenticating prophetic messages. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-13-commentary)

### v. 2 — *"…and if the sign or wonder comes about, but he says, 'Let us follow other gods'…"*

- The key point across all commentators: **the sign actually comes true** — yet the prophet must still be rejected. The accuracy of the prophecy is like a "lure on a fish hook," enticing people to follow idols. False prophets can perform true signs and wonders. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-13-commentary)

- Guzik: "The display of supernatural power – even real supernatural power – does not prove that a message comes from God." 2 Thessalonians 2:9 says the lawless one comes "according to the working of Satan, with all power, signs, and lying wonders." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-13/)

- The Pulpit Commentary explains: the mere fact that the prophet seeks to seduce people from Jehovah proves him an impostor. The sign could only be one of "those lying signs and wonders after the working of Satan," permitted by God to test fidelity. They already had God's Word; no teaching contradicting it, however apparently authenticated, could be from Him (cf. Gal. 1:8-9; 1 John 4:1). (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/13.htm)

- Deere (cited in Precept Austin): "Miracles happen in many religions because Satan uses false religions and false prophets to deceive the world (cf. 2 Cor. 11:13-15). … The standard of truth is the Word of God." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-13-commentary)

### v. 3 — *"…you must not listen … For the LORD your God is testing you…"*

- The command "do not listen" (שָׁמַע, shama) means more than passive hearing — it means "do not hear and heed/obey." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-13-commentary)

- **Testing**: God is not the source of evil, but He uses evil agents to test His people's hearts. The test reveals whether they love Him with all heart and soul. Guzik quotes Meyer: "God proves us — not that He may learn aught of us which He did not know before, but that He may reveal us to ourselves." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-13/)

- Gill: If they were swayed by such a prophet despite the miracles, it would prove they did not cordially love the Lord. Conversely, remaining steadfast proves sincere attachment. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/13.htm)

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic note** (Guzik/Enduring Word): The emphasis is that believers must test all spiritual claims, not be "sign-chasers." Jesus said signs "follow those who believe" (Mark 16:17) — believers follow Jesus, not signs. Yet Guzik affirms God may still speak through dreams today, though never against Scripture or with equal authority. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-13/)

### v. 4 — *"You are to follow the LORD your God and fear Him. Keep His commandments… serve Him and hold fast to Him."*

- This verse lists **six actions** by which Israel demonstrates love for God: walk after (follow) the LORD, fear Him, keep His commandments, obey His voice, serve Him, and cleave (hold fast) to Him. The Hebrew for "cleave" (דָּבַק, dabaq) is the same word used for the marital bond (Gen. 2:24). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/13.htm; https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-13-commentary)

- Gill explains that "fear Him" means a filial (child-like), reverential fear, not servile terror. "Obey His voice" may be understood as the voice of Christ, the Angel who went before them (Ex. 23:21). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/13.htm)

### v. 5 — *"…must be put to death, because he has advocated rebellion … So you must purge the evil from among you."*

- **The death penalty**: Under Israel's theocratic government, heresy and leading others to apostasy was a capital crime — "high treason" against the Divine King, as Gill puts it ("spoken revolt against the Lord"). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/13.htm)

- **Ellicott** notes that this law justifies Elijah's execution of the prophets of Baal at Carmel (1 Kings 18:40). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-13.html)

- **New Covenant application (Guzik)**: "Under the new covenant, God has not commanded the formation of Christian nations along the same pattern as He did with biblical Israel. … Neither the church nor the state has the same divine command to execute false teachers. Instead, false teachers should be noted and avoided (Rom. 16:17; 1 Tim. 6:3-5; 2 John 1:10-11)." Guzik notes that earlier commentator Trapp (mid-1600s) believed the Christian magistrate still held power "to inflict capital punishment on gross heretics; such as was Servetus at Geneva" — but Guzik distances himself from this view. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-13/)

- **Reformed note (Ligonier)**: "Civil authorities have been given the right to bear the sword by God Himself (Rom. 13:1–7), so they have a kind of 'divine' authority that has been delegated to them. … Christ, on the other hand, possesses divine authority inherently according to His divine nature. He never fails to do justice." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/charges-of-blasphemy-refuted)

- **Brethren view (Grant)**: The accurate prophecy "only proved that he was influenced by satanic power." The death penalty was required "only by the death of the false prophet could the evil be put away from Israel's midst." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/deuteronomy-13.html)

---

## Verses 6–11: The Close Relative or Friend

### v. 6 — *"If your very own brother, or your son or daughter, or the wife you embrace, or your closest friend secretly entices you…"*

- The list moves from closest kinship outward: full brother ("son of your mother"), children, wife ("of your bosom" — object of tenderest affection), and friend "who is as your own soul" (one you love as yourself). The Pulpit Commentary notes the Hebrew word for friend (רֵעַ) conveys delight — a companion one truly delights in. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/13.htm)

- The enticement is **secret** (בַּסֵּתֶר, baseter) — done privately, when alone, making it harder to detect and more insidious. Gill notes: "So Satan took the opportunity of Eve being alone when he attacked her with his temptation, and the same method is taken by his children." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/13.htm)

- **Ellicott** observes that the principle is reproduced in the Gospel: "He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me" (Matt. 10:37) and Luke 14:26. "It is impossible to deny or escape the identity of the Lord Jesus with the Jehovah of the Old Testament." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-13.html)

### v. 7 — *"…the gods of the peoples around you, whether near or far…"*

- The description covers the totality of pagan deities — from neighboring Edomites, Moabites, and Canaanites to far-off Babylonians and Persians. Gill notes the phrase "from one end of the earth even unto the other" shows the universality of idolatry in those times. Jarchi (Rashi) interpreted this of the sun, moon, and host of heaven — the most ancient and common form of idolatry. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/13.htm)

### v. 8 — *"…you must not yield to him or listen to him. Show him no pity, and do not spare him or shield him."*

- **Four prohibitions** are piled up for emphasis: do not consent, do not listen, do not pity, do not spare, do not conceal. The accumulation of terms "serves to make the injunction more solemn and impressive" (Pulpit). (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/13.htm)

- Gill: "neither shall thou conceal him" means not hiding the person or the sin, but making both public, bringing him before the civil magistrate. No excusing or extenuating. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/13.htm)

### v. 9 — *"Instead, you must surely kill him. Your hand must be the first against him…"*

- **"Surely kill"** is a doubled Hebrew verb for emphasis ("kill kill"). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-13-commentary)

- The enticed person — the one tempted — must cast the first stone. Ellicott says this was "a law tending to prevent false accusation. Where the witness is obliged to carry out himself, or to aid in carrying out, the sentence he demands, secret accusation is impossible; and it is far less easy to pervert the law in order to prosecute a private quarrel." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-13.html)

- Gill provides fascinating detail from the Mishnah (Sanhedrin 7:10): the Jewish courts would set up a sting operation — the enticed person would bring two witnesses hidden behind a hedge who could hear but not be seen. If the enticer repeated his call to idolatry when confronted, he was taken to the Sanhedrin. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/13.htm)

### v. 10 — *"Stone him to death for trying to turn you away from the LORD your God…"*

- Stoning was the prescribed method of execution. The reason again invokes redemption from Egypt — God's redeeming act made apostasy not just disobedience but ingratitude against the Redeemer. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/13.htm)

### v. 11 — *"Then all Israel will hear and be afraid, and will never again do such a wicked thing…"*

- The public nature of the punishment served as a deterrent. Kalland (cited by Guzik): "This extreme punishment is expected to produce good results. Though many modern sociologists declare that punishment — especially capital punishment — is no deterrent to crime, the message Moses proclaimed as the Word of God says that it would be a deterrent." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-13/)

- **Brethren view (Grant)**: "Such swift judgment as this would awaken Israel to 'hear and fear' … Such false worship is just as abominable to God now as it was in Israel, though today is the day of grace, when God delays His judgment in desire that people will judge themselves and be saved." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/deuteronomy-13.html)

- Merrill (cited by Guzik) notes the sad reality: "Unfortunately, the injunction must seldom if ever have been carried out. Over and over again Israel and Judah were unfaithful to the Lord." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-13/)

---

## Verses 12–18: The Apostate City

### v. 12 — *"If, regarding one of the cities the LORD your God is giving you to inhabit, you hear it said…"*

- The third case escalates to a whole city. Ellicott notes the only biblical case approximating this is **Gibeah** (Judges 19–20), where the abominations were likely connected to idolatry (cf. Hos. 9:9; 10:9). In Judges 20:13, Israel demanded "the men, the children of Belial" be handed over — language directly echoing this chapter. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-13.html)

### v. 13 — *"…that wicked men have arisen from among you and have led the people of their city astray…"*

- **"Wicked men"** is literally "children of Belial" (בְּנֵי בְלִיַּעַל, bene beliyya'al). Ellicott notes this is the *first occurrence* of the phrase in Scripture (Judges 19:22 is the second). Modern scholars generally explain it as "worthlessness" (from בְּלִי = without, and יַעַל = profit/worth). Rashi curiously explained it as "destroyers of the yoke" (of Jehovah). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-13.html)

- Clarke (cited by Guzik): "lawless men; — persons good for nothing to themselves or others, and capable of nothing but mischief." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-13/)

- The verb "led astray" (נָדַח, nadach) in the Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary is translated as "to drive or force away," implying strong persuasion. The text assumes the wicked men have *successfully* seduced the inhabitants — not merely attempted. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-13-commentary)

### v. 14 — *"…then you must inquire, investigate, and interrogate thoroughly…"*

- **Threefold investigation**: "inquire" (דָּרַשׁ, darash — make inquisition, require proof), "search out" (חָקַר, chaqar), and "ask diligently" (שָׁאַל, sha'al). The Garner-Howes Commentary emphasizes: "The language denotes a full judicial inquiry. Action could be taken only after the facts were fully substantiated. … The length of time required for such a judicial inquiry would also allow ample time for repentance." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/deuteronomy-13.html)

- Guzik points to Joshua 22:10-34 as a positive example: when the eastern tribes built an altar, Israel prepared for war but investigated first, discovering the altar was a memorial, not for pagan worship. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-13/)

- Gill notes that according to Maimonides, this was a matter for the Great Sanhedrin of 71 in Jerusalem. They would send two disciples of the wise men to admonish the city and call them to repentance before any military action. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/13.htm)

### v. 15 — *"…you must surely put the inhabitants of that city to the sword. Devote to destruction all its people and livestock."*

- **"Devote to destruction"** (חָרַם, charam; LXX: ἀναθεματίζω, anathematizo) is the language of the *herem* ban — the same treatment commanded for Canaanite cities. Poole (cited by Guzik): "The very same punishment which was inflicted upon the cities of the cursed Canaanites, to whom having made themselves equal in sin, it is but fit and just that God should equal them in punishment." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-13/)

- Thompson (cited by Guzik): "Theirs was a corporate guilt and, as so often in the Old Testament, they were judged corporately." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-13/)

- Ellicott cross-references Judges 20:48: "The men of every city, the beast, and all that were found." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-13.html)

### v. 16 — *"…gather all its plunder in the middle of the public square, and completely burn the city… as a whole burnt offering to the LORD… a mound of ruins forever, never to be rebuilt."*

- Everything was to be burned as a "whole burnt offering" (כָּלִיל, kalil) to the LORD — total consecration by destruction. Precept Austin notes the irony: in most offerings, animals had to be without blemish, "but here the 'blemish-filled' city was to be 'offered.'" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-13-commentary)

- Clarke (cited by Guzik): "As God did not permit them to take the spoils of these idolatrous cities, they could be under no temptation to make war upon them. … How few religious wars would there ever have been in the world had they been regulated by this principle: 'Thou shalt neither extend thy territory, nor take any spoils!'" This prevented anyone from profiting materially by declaring a city apostate. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-13/)

- **"Heap forever"** — the Hebrew word is תֵּל (tel), which is the archaeological term for a mound of accumulated ruins. Kalland: "This doom, which goes contrary to the common practice of rebuilding towns on the ruins of the site, as the stratigraphic remains of tells in the Middle East plainly show, indicates how serious the Lord considered any defection from him." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-13/)

- Ellicott: "So Gibeah was treated (Judges 20:40)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-13.html)

### v. 17 — *"Nothing devoted to destruction shall cling to your hands, so that the LORD will turn from His fierce anger, grant you mercy…"*

- This echoes the story of **Achan** (Joshua 7), who kept devoted things from Jericho and brought disaster on Israel. Ellicott: "We seem to hear an echo of this verse in the close of the story of Achan (Joshua 7:26)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-13.html)

- The phrase "cling to your hands" (דָּבַק, dabaq — the same word as "hold fast" to God in v. 4) creates a powerful contrast: Israel must cling to God, not to devoted things. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-13-commentary)

- Gill: "All being devoted to destruction, was cursed, and brought a curse upon the man that should make it his own property, as Achan did." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/13.htm)

### v. 18 — *"…because you obey the LORD your God, keeping all His commandments … doing what is right in the eyes of the LORD your God."*

- Obedience to these severe commands is presented as the pathway to blessing — mercy, compassion, and multiplication according to the patriarchal promises. This demonstrates that faithfulness to God, not ethnic or national ties, is the ultimate priority. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-13/)

- Guzik closes by summarizing G. Campbell Morgan's four recurring seductions from true worship: (1) curiosity (Deut. 12:29-32), (2) signs and wonders (13:1-5), (3) enticements of human affection (13:6-11), and (4) failure to discipline/confront false teaching (13:12-18). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-13/)

## Tradition-Specific Notes

### Reformed / Baptist

- **Gill (Reformed Baptist)**: Treats the passage as straightforward divine law for Israel's theocracy. He emphasizes that no sign, however impressive, can validate a message that contradicts God's revealed law. The death penalty is just because it is "high treason" against the Divine King who redeemed Israel. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/13.htm)

- **Ligonier (Reformed)**: In a devotional on Deuteronomy 13:1-5, the focus is on the danger of false prophets and the reality that civil authorities bear the sword by God's delegation (Rom. 13:1-7). Christ, however, possesses divine authority inherently and will bring perfect justice where earthly justice fails. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/charges-of-blasphemy-refuted)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)

- Guzik emphasizes that supernatural signs do not prove divine origin — a crucial point for charismatic contexts where signs and wonders are valued. He warns: "Those who are immediately convinced at the apparent presence of supernatural power are in danger of being deceived." Yet he also affirms God may still speak through dreams today, though "never against the Bible or never equal to the Bible's authority or importance." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-13/)

- The Precept Austin commentary (broadly evangelical with charismatic sympathies) repeatedly stresses: "Signs don't test truth. Truth tests signs!" It connects the passage to end-times warnings about false signs (Matt. 24:24; 2 Thess. 2:9-11; Rev. 13:13-14). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-13-commentary)

### Brethren / Grant's Commentary

- Grant draws explicit parallels to church discipline: "If in the Church of God evil doctrine or wicked moral practice raises its head … If it is found only in an individual, that person must be put away from fellowship. If such evil is protected by any gathering, that gathering" [must be judged]. The New Testament application is separation from false teachers, not execution. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/deuteronomy-13.html)

### Anglican (Ellicott)

- Ellicott acknowledges the law "may seem harsh" but insists "its principle is reproduced in the Gospel" in Christ's call to love Him above all family ties (Matt. 10:37; Luke 14:26). He finds the identity of Jesus with the Jehovah of the Old Testament "impossible to deny or escape." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-13.html)

## What Was Not Found

- **Catholic and Orthodox readings**: No accessible pages from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org were found for Deuteronomy 13 specifically.
- **Methodist/Wesleyan sources** (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com): No accessible pages found.
- **Lutheran sources** (lcms.org, 1517.org): No accessible pages found.
- **Modern scholarship** (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org): The NET Bible note on v. 1 was cited through Precept Austin but full NET notes were not retrieved.
- **Prosperity / Word of Faith / Hyper-grace readings**: No accessible pages found from the approved sites.
